newsitem.title: BELGIUM: South Africa against the clock for trade deal.
newsitem.headline: South Africa against the clock for trade deal.

text.p: South Africa may still have a chance of partial membership of a lucrative trade treaty with the European Union, officials said on Wednesday, but they are running against the clock to complete negotiations before an April deadline.
The EU and South Africa ended two days of trade talks in Brussels on Wednesday with "progress but no agreement", the European Commission said.
"We made progress on South Africa's partial accession to the Lome treaty and some on bilateral relations," a Commission spokesman said.

The spokesman said EU and South African trade negotiators had agreed broad terms for South Africa's partial accession to the Lome Convention -- which governs EU relations with African, Caribbean and Pacific (ACP) nations -- and also a timetable for bilateral trade talks.
But the terms of south Africa's Lome membership have to be agreed before an EU/ACP meeting in April or the deal could be sidelined for another two years.
Partial Lome membership would give South Africa full political representation in the ACP but Pretoria would not be eligible for ACP development aid.
South Africa already receives over 125 million Ecus ($143 million) a year from the European Union in bilateral aid.
Pretoria would also be eligible for European Development Fund projects and be allowed to tender for lucrative ACP contracts.
The Commission spokesman said South Africa and the EU had also agreed to hold a ministerial meeting later this year to review bilateral trade.

The EU does not want to grant South Africa the substantial trade benefits it offers ACP countries for fear Pretoria's exports would crush those of the 70-member bloc -- many of them former colonies of the 15 EU nations.
Instead, the EU wants a free-trade deal with South Africa that would exclude certain agricultural products but open a vast new market for European exports.

South Africa, however, has been holding out for a better deal that would include more tariff-free access to European markets for its agricultural exports and also has reservations over what a free-trade deal would mean for its regional partners.

South Africa and the EU have been at odds over what kind of a trade deal to establish since Pretoria emerged from years of apartheid isolation and have been haggling over terms for more than two years.
